title: Separable Counterexamples to Complementary Quantum Correlations, and Why Random Search Missed Them
abstract: The complementary quantum correlations (CQC) relation bounds the sum of two classical mutual informations, obtained from local mutually unbiased measurements, by the quantum mutual information of the premeasurement state. We refute it. Separable rank-two counterexamples exist in every local dimension pair \(m\times n\) with \(m,n\ge3\), with closed-form excess at least \(1/(8m^2n^2)\) nats, and in every qubit--qudit pair \(2\times n\) with \(n\ge3\) except \(n=3,5\); every covered pair also admits full-rank separable counterexamples. We then analyse the two residual qubit--qudit dimensions. A dimension-free entropy envelope replaces the natural quadratic majorant and lowers the requirement for closing the equal-prior orthogonal two-ray family from a triangular-discrimination bound \(S\le8/3\) to \(S\le3.8265583\ldots\); the associated gate matrix has trace exactly two, so its spectral test collapses to a single eigenvalue-free scalar; and the exact identity \(X=1-4\operatorname{Var}(c)\) turns the prime-Fourier full-spark barrier into a variance bound. A \(128\)-bit interval cover then closes that family at \(2\times3\) with gap at least \(0.012021\) nats, and at \(2\times5\) an exact saturator attaining \(S=(14+2\sqrt5)/5\) refutes three competing routes. We also give a state-dependent corrected inequality that is universal, and show it is incomparable with CQC already at \(2\times2\). Finally we quantify why the original searches had essentially no power to find these states: the violating set is a sliver against the low-rank boundary, the witness lies \(7.3\) standard deviations below the Hilbert--Schmidt mean, the bases must be aligned to about nine degrees (\(\sim10^{-21}\) of frames), and extrapolating the sample minimum demands \(10^{10}\) to \(10^{18}\) samples against the \(10^7\) ever run.
summary: This paper rigorously refutes the Complementary Quantum Correlations (CQC) inequality by constructing explicit counterexamples using separable states. The authors develop advanced mathematical tools to prove these violations across many dimension pairs. It highlights that detecting such subtle correlations requires highly targeted theoretical methods rather than brute-force numerical sampling.
main_problem: The paper refutes the Complementary Quantum Correlations (CQC) relation, which bounds quantum mutual information using local measurements.
main_result: Separable counterexamples to CQC are constructed for most dimension pairs ($m 	imes n$ with $m,n\ge3$), showing that entanglement is not required for the violation.
method: The authors use rigorous mathematical constructions, including closed-form proofs, entropy envelopes, and variance bounds derived from analyzing specific quantum correlation measures.
model_or_system: The study concerns bipartite quantum systems $ho_{AB}$ on $\mathbb{C}^d \otimes \mathbb{C}^d$, involving local measurements using mutually unbiased bases (MUBs).
key_observables: The CQC gap, $G(ho) = I(A : B)_ho - I(Q_A : Q_B) - I(R_A : R_B)$, and the triangular-discrimination sum ($S$).
important_parameters: Local dimensions $m$ and $n$, with specific focus on pairs like $2 	imes n$ for $n\ge3$.
main_assumptions: The analysis distinguishes between rigorously proven results (closed form) and the limitations of previous numerical searches, which were shown to have negligible power.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometry of the violating set as a 'sliver' against the low-rank boundary in state space, and show how violation survival depends on local unitary misalignment angles.
paper_structure: The paper systematically refutes CQC by constructing counterexamples for various dimensions, developing new mathematical machinery (like dimension-free entropy envelopes), and finally quantifying why previous random searches failed to find these states.
why_interesting: It provides deep theoretical insights into the fundamental limits of quantum correlations beyond entanglement measures, which is crucial for understanding device characterization and resource quantification in quantum information protocols.
